summary: Specifies how to put compressed DV video, as defined in IEC 61834, into RTP packets. It obsoletes RFC 3189.

eli5.summary: DV is a way of squeezing video, popular in digital camcorders. This describes how to cut that video into packets and label them for streaming, and replaces an older description.

subtitle: How to carry DV camcorder video, and optionally its audio, in RTP packets using whole 80-byte DIF blocks.

tldr.problem: DV is a compressed video and audio format designed for recording on tape, and it needs a standard way to be streamed over IP with the Real-Time Transport Protocol (RTP).
tldr.mechanism: The stream is cut into 80-byte DIF blocks and whole blocks are placed straight after the RTP header, with no extra payload header. All blocks in a packet come from one video frame, and the RTP timestamp tells frames apart.
tldr.outcome: RFC 6469 is a Proposed Standard that obsoletes RFC 3189. It adds SMPTE 370M 100 Mbit/s HDTV formats, offer/answer guidance and a revised media type registration.

today: RFC 6469 is a Proposed Standard published in December 2011. It obsoletes RFC 3189, and the unit metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it.

sections.title: What Is Being Packetized
sections.content:
This document specifies how to encapsulate Digital Video (DV) data streams into the Real-Time Transport Protocol (RTP, RFC 3550). DV compression was designed as a recording format for helical-scan magnetic tape. The consumer standards are IEC 61883 and IEC 61834, and the professional extensions are SMPTE 314M and 370M.

The payload format covers six IEC video formats: SD-VCR (525/60, 625/50), HD-VCR (1125/60, 1250/50) and SDL-VCR (525/60, 625/50). It also covers eight SMPTE formats: 314M at 25 Mbit/s and 50 Mbit/s (each in 525/60 and 625/50) and 370M at 100 Mbit/s (1080/60i, 1080/50i, 720/60p, 720/50p).

DV that uses MPEG2 encoding is out of scope here, because RFC 2250 already defines an RTP payload for MPEG2. The RFC uses IEC and SMPTE terminology throughout and tells readers to consult those standards for definitions.
sections.eli5: Camcorders record video in a special squashed format called DV. This RFC explains how to send that squashed video over the internet in small pieces.

sections.title: The DV Data Structure
sections.content:
DV uses only DCT compression inside each frame, unlike MPEG video, which also compresses across frames. A picture is divided into DCT super blocks, then 27 DCT macro blocks per super block, then DCT blocks of 8x8 pixels for each of Y, Cb and Cr. Audio is PCM, sampled at 32 kHz, 44.1 kHz or 48 kHz, with up to 8 channels.

For transport, a frame is divided into DIF sequences, and each sequence is a whole number of DIF blocks. A DIF block is 80 bytes and is the basic unit for everything in a DV stream. It starts with a 3-byte ID header giving its type and position in the sequence. Five types exist: DIF sequence header, Subcode, Video Auxiliary (VAUX), Audio and Video. An audio DIF block holds 5 bytes of Audio Auxiliary (AAUX) data and 72 bytes of audio.
sections.eli5: A DV movie is built from tiny identical boxes that are each 80 bytes long. Each box has a label saying whether it holds picture, sound, or notes about the picture.

sections.title: RTP Header Usage
sections.content:
Each packet starts with the normal RTP header, and this payload format needs no additional payload-specific header. Three fields have DV-specific meaning.

The payload type is assigned dynamically by means outside this document. If several DV encoding formats are used in one session, each needs its own payload type, and the sender MUST switch payload type when the format changes.

The timestamp is a 32-bit 90 kHz value for when the first data in the frame was sampled. All packets of one frame MUST carry the same timestamp, and it SHOULD advance by a multiple of the nominal frame interval, for example 3003 for 525-60 and 3600 for 625-50. For the 720-line systems, the increase shown covers the time of two video frames.

The marker bit is set to one on the last packet of a frame and MUST be zero otherwise. Receivers MUST NOT rely on it to detect a new frame, because the last packet may be lost. Frame changes MUST be detected from a change in the RTP timestamp.
sections.eli5: Every envelope from the same picture gets the same time stamp, like pages stamped with the same date. When the date changes, the receiver knows a new picture has started.

sections.title: Payload Structure and Bundling
sections.content:
Whole DIF blocks go into the payload right after the RTP header. Any number of blocks may share a packet, but they MUST all come from the same video frame, even if space remains. The payload length is therefore always a multiple of 80 bytes.

Audio and video can travel bundled in one RTP stream, or unbundled in separate streams. The choice is part of the dynamic payload type assignment and MUST NOT change during the session. In a bundled stream, DIF blocks are packed in the order they were encoded. In an unbundled stream, the video stream carries only header, subcode, video and VAUX blocks, and audio goes in another stream with its own payload type. When audio and video are unbundled, any DIF sequence header and subcode blocks MUST be sent in the video stream. It is RECOMMENDED that unbundled audio be repackaged into an ordinary audio payload format (DAT12, L16, L20) to interoperate with receivers that cannot handle DV.

No SDP parameters describe things like frame rate or aspect ratio, since listing every combination would be too large. Instead the sender MUST transmit at least those VAUX and audio DIF blocks that carry the source and source control packs needed for decoding.

A sender MAY lower the frame rate by dropping video and VAUX blocks for some frames, but the timestamp MUST still advance for the dropped frames. It MAY also skip blocks for unchanged parts of the image, and receivers SHOULD conceal missing blocks, for example by repeating the block from the previous image.
sections.eli5: Packets are packed with whole 80-byte boxes, and never mix two pictures. Sound can ride in the same truck as the picture, or in its own truck.

sections.title: Media Types and SDP Parameters
sections.content:
The RFC registers media types video/DV and audio/DV. The required parameter encode names the DV format, for example SD-VCR/525-60, 314M-50/625-50 or 370M/1080-60i. The values 306M/525-60 and 306M/625-50 are kept for backward compatibility. The optional parameter audio is bundled or none, and defaults to none.

In SDP, the media type goes in the m= line and the subtype DV goes in a=rtpmap with a clock rate that MUST be 90000. Other parameters go into a=fmtp as encode=... and, optionally, audio=.... If audio is absent, audio MUST NOT be bundled.

For offer/answer (RFC 3264), each encode type MUST use a separate payload type number, and unknown parameters in an offer MUST be ignored and left out of the answer. For unbundled streams the SDP grouping framework (RFC 5888) can associate the audio and video.
sections.eli5: Before the show starts, both sides swap a short note saying which kind of DV they will use and whether sound is in the same stream.

sections.title: Security and Congestion Control
sections.content:
Packets are subject to the security considerations of RTP and the RTP profile in use. Confidentiality comes from encryption, and because compression is end-to-end, encryption can be applied after compression without conflict. The RFC notes the usual denial-of-service concern for codecs with uneven decoding cost, and says this encoding does not show significant non-uniformity.

A receiver can also be overloaded simply by too many packets. For multicast, the RFC points to source-filtering mechanisms in IGMPv3, MLDv2 and their lightweight variants, and to Source-Specific Multicast (RFC 4607). Congestion control follows the general rules for RTP data in RFC 3550 and any applicable profile such as RFC 3551.
sections.eli5: If you want to keep the video private, scramble it after squashing it. In big group broadcasts, a receiver can also choose which senders it listens to so it is not flooded.

sections.title: Changes From RFC 3189
sections.content:
RFC 6469 obsoletes RFC 3189. The changes are: SMPTE 306M is kept only for backward interoperability, since SMPTE 314M covers it; the SMPTE 370M 100 Mbit/s HDTV formats were added; a reference to Source-Specific Multicast was added; the case where a sender omits subcode DIF blocks was clarified; offer/answer considerations were added; and the media type registration form was revised under RFC 4855.

For interoperability, RFC 3189 treated 306M and 314M as different encodings. This document says the 306M definition SHOULD NOT be used and 314M SHOULD be used instead. An offer MAY include 306M from a legacy system and receivers SHOULD support it, and an application MAY treat a 306M stream as 314M. The RFC also notes that the SDP examples in RFC 3189 used a=fmtp incorrectly.
sections.eli5: This is a cleaned-up second edition. It adds sharper high-definition video types and fixes mistakes in the examples of the first edition.
